steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our NLP paper on CoAnnotating, a framework that splits data annotation work between humans and LLMs based on the LLM's uncertainty. Explain why labeled data still matters, how prior work compares LLMs and human annotators, and what our framework and results contribute.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Labeled data still matters despite LLM zero-shot ability
- Human annotation and its challenges; LLMs as annotators
- Mixed evidence and the competitor framing
- CoAnnotating: human-LLM collaboration as resource allocation via uncertainty
- Results and insights

- Human annotation / LLM annotators
  - experts or crowd workers (cite)
  - challenges: cost of recruiting and training annotators, inconsistency, subjectivity (cite)
  - recent work: LLMs vs crowd workers (cite); ChatGPT could replace large-scale manual annotation (cite)
  - sometimes LLM annotation quality beats humans on certain tasks (cite)
  - much lower cost -> potential for cost efficiency
- Mixed evidence
  - LLM zero-shot falls short of humans on more difficult, pragmatic tasks (cite)
  - caution advised (cite)
  - prior work: humans and LLMs as competitors, LLM labels as replacement, not collaboration
- CoAnnotating
  - motivated by Human-LLM collaboration
  - balance complementary profiles: annotation quality and cost
  - resource allocation perspective
  - model confidence as reliable signal of expected performance, following prior work (cite)
  - inverse of uncertainty -> confidence in allocating a datapoint to the LLM
  - instance-level expertise beyond task-level -> more informed allocation than coarse dataset-level
- Results
  - uncertainty-based allocation more efficient and accurate than random allocation baseline
  - LLM confidence scores generally well-calibrated, not always reliable

  - nuanced tasks: quality vs cost tradeoff inevitable

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Labeled data plays a critical role in building benchmarks and developing models for Natural Language Processing (NLP). Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have shown strong zero-shot performance in many tasks, like question answering, reasoning, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. But fine-tuned language models still get better results than LLMs on most of these tasks. So collecting labeled data for training and fine-tuning models is still valuable. Instead of deploying LLMs directly for downstream uses, it is worth investigating how researchers can use the zero-shot capability of LLMs to label text data, so that they can construct high-quality datasets and improve the performance of fine-tuned models.

Usually researchers recruit human annotators, for example experts or crowd workers, to do data annotation. Manual annotation has some challenges, like the high cost of recruiting and training annotators, inconsistent annotation and human subjectivity. Recent work looked at how LLMs perform compared to crowd workers, and the results showed that LLMs like ChatGPT could replace large-scale manual annotation. In some cases the annotation quality of LLMs is even better than human annotators on certain tasks. Since annotating with LLMs costs much less than crowd workers, LLMs are seen as having great potential to make the data annotation process more cost efficient. However, some studies also show that LLMs' zero-shot performance is worse than human performance on more difficult and pragmatic tasks. These studies suggest that practitioners should be careful when they use LLMs to annotate data.

- Competitor framing -> collaboration
  - prior works: humans vs LLMs as competitors; LLM labels as replacement; no efficient collaboration
  - Human-LLM collaboration motivates this work
- CoAnnotating
  - balance complementary profiles (annotation quality, cost)
  - resource allocation perspective
  - model confidence as reliable signal for expected performance, following prior work
  - inverse of uncertainty -> confidence in allocating a datapoint to the LLM
  - instance-level expertise beyond task-level; more informed than coarse dataset-level
- Results
  - uncertainty-based allocation beats random allocation baseline (efficiency, accuracy)
  - LLM confidence generally well-calibrated, not always reliable
  - straightforward tasks (topic understanding): outsource some work at human-level performance
  - nuanced tasks: quality/cost tradeoff inevitable

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Labeled data plays a critical role in building benchmarks and developing models for Natural Language Processing (NLP). Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have shown strong zero-shot performance in many tasks, like question answering, reasoning, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. But fine-tuned language models still get better results than LLMs on most of these tasks. So collecting labeled data for training and fine-tuning models is still valuable. Instead of deploying LLMs directly for downstream uses, it is worth investigating how researchers can use the zero-shot capability of LLMs to label text data, so that they can construct high-quality datasets and improve the performance of fine-tuned models.

Usually researchers recruit human annotators, for example experts or crowd workers, to do data annotation. Manual annotation has some challenges, like the high cost of recruiting and training annotators, inconsistent annotation and human subjectivity. Recent work looked at how LLMs perform compared to crowd workers, and the results showed that LLMs like ChatGPT could replace large-scale manual annotation. In some cases the annotation quality of LLMs is even better than human annotators on certain tasks. Since annotating with LLMs costs much less than crowd workers, LLMs are seen as having great potential to make the data annotation process more cost efficient. However, some studies also show that LLMs' zero-shot performance is worse than human performance on more difficult and pragmatic tasks. These studies suggest that practitioners should be careful when they use LLMs to annotate data.

These prior works see humans and LLMs as competitors. They measure the accuracy of LLM labels as a replacement for human annotation, and they do not consider how humans and LLMs could collaborate efficiently. This Human-LLM collaboration is what motivates our work. We propose the CoAnnotating framework, which tries to balance the complementary profiles of humans and LLMs in terms of their annotation quality and cost. We approach the problem of Human-LLM co-annotation from a resource allocation perspective. Following prior work, we use model confidence as a reliable signal for the expected performance of the model. When we consider giving a datapoint to an LLM to annotate, we can use the inverse of the model's uncertainty to estimate how confident we are in that allocation. In CoAnnotating we quantify the annotating expertise of LLMs at the instance-level (how well LLMs can annotate the given data point) and not only at the task-level (how LLMs perform overall on each dataset). This fine-grained and contextualized instance-level view lets us make a more informed allocation decision than broad and coarse dataset-level expertise.

We show that our method, which uses the uncertainty of responses, gives a more efficient and more accurate work allocation than the random allocation baseline. Our results also show that the confidence scores that LLMs generate are generally well-calibrated, but they are not always reliable. For more straightforward tasks like topic understanding, some annotation work can be outsourced and still reach human-level performance. For more nuanced tasks, on the other hand, there is an inevitable tradeoff between annotation quality and annotation cost. Our framework gives a guide for allocating AI and human efforts effectively in collaborative annotation, and it also gives key insights into what LLMs can do and into the nature of the tasks and data that are still outside what they can do.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Labeled data plays a critical role in establishing benchmarks and developing models for Natural Language Processing (NLP). Although Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have demonstrated strong zero-shot performance in various tasks such as question answering, reasoning, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition, fine-tuned language models still outperform LLMs on most of these tasks [1,2,3]. Collecting labeled data for model training and fine-tuning is therefore still valuable. Rather than deploying LLMs directly for downstream uses, it is worthwhile to investigate how researchers can leverage LLMs' zero-shot capability in labeling text data to construct high-quality datasets and improve the performance of fine-tuned models.

Typically, researchers recruit human annotators such as experts or crowd workers to perform data annotation [4,5]. Challenges in manual annotation include the high cost of recruiting and training annotators, annotation inconsistency, and human subjectivity [6,7]. Recent work explored how LLMs perform relative to crowd workers [8], and results showed that LLMs like ChatGPT could replace large-scale manual annotation [9,10]. In some cases, LLMs' annotation quality even outperforms human annotators on certain tasks [11]. Given their much lower annotation cost compared to crowd workers, LLMs are considered to have great potential for increasing the cost efficiency of the data annotation process. However, some studies also show that LLMs' zero-shot performance falls short of human performance on more difficult and pragmatic tasks [12,13], and suggest that practitioners use caution when using LLMs to annotate data [14,9]. Such prior works view humans and LLMs as competitors, measuring the accuracy of LLM labels as a replacement for human annotation, rather than considering how humans and LLMs might collaborate efficiently. It is this Human-LLM collaboration that motivates our work. We propose the CoAnnotating framework, which aims to balance the complementary profiles of humans and LLMs in terms of their respective annotation quality and cost. Our work tackles Human-LLM co-annotation from a resource allocation perspective. Following [15], [16] and [12], we consider model confidence a reliable signal of the model's expected performance. When allocating a given datapoint for an LLM to annotate, we can use the inverse of the model's uncertainty to estimate our confidence in that allocation. Under CoAnnotating, we quantify LLMs' annotating expertise at the instance-level (estimating how well LLMs can annotate the given data point) beyond the task-level (evaluating how LLMs perform overall on each dataset). This fine-grained and contextualized instance-level perspective allows a more informed allocation decision than broad and coarse dataset-level expertise.

We show that our proposed method, which uses the uncertainty of responses, achieves a more efficient and more accurate work allocation than the random allocation baseline. Our results also show that the confidence scores generated by LLMs are generally well-calibrated but not always reliable. For more straightforward tasks like topic understanding, it is possible to outsource some annotation work while achieving human-level performance. For more nuanced tasks, on the other hand, a tradeoff between annotation quality and annotation cost is inevitable. Our framework establishes a guide for effectively allocating AI and human efforts in collaborative annotation, and in doing so provides key insights into the capacities of LLMs as well as the nature of the tasks and data that remain outside these capacities.
